member.name: P:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Data.SubdlSqliteContext.Gate
member.summary:
The one gate every read and write goes through.
NOT optional, and not a performance choice. A is single-threaded by contract: a second operation started while another is in flight throws InvalidOperationException ("A second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed"). The plugin shares ONE context across all registries, the scheduled tasks and the API endpoints, and the configuration page polls /Plugins/SubdlSync/Stats every 10 seconds while a worker writes — so without this gate the failure is not hypothetical, it is a matter of timing.
The previous engine held thread-safe collection handles and needed no such gate. This is the one behavioural difference the format change introduced that the callers cannot see, which is why it lives here rather than at every call site.

member.name: F:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Data.SubdlSqliteContext.BatchFloor
member.summary:
How many writes may accumulate before a batch commits on its own.
The floor exists so the change tracker never walks an unbounded set: Entity Framework runs change detection over every tracked row on each SaveChanges, and the row cache holds whole areas. On the largest install measured (11 153 embedded rows, 1 201 media rows) 500 keeps that walk cheap while collapsing a 14 000-write scan into roughly 28 commits.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Data.SubdlSqliteContext.BeginBatch
member.summary:
Opens a batch: writes made until accumulate and commit together instead of one transaction per row.
WHY this exists: a single row used to cost one commit, and a commit is a platter sync. Measured live (08.10.2026): a library scan issued 9 644 writes at a flat 45 ms each — 496 s of wall time for a pass that changed nothing. The upload and download pipelines write through the same path, so the cost was never the seeder's alone.
READ-AFTER-WRITE IS PRESERVED WITHOUT THE COMMIT: readers go through the per-area row cache, which the areas maintain in place, so a value written a moment ago is visible to this context before it is durable. What changes is when the FILE receives it — an independent context (the config page holds one) sees it at the next flush, up to rows later.
Callers pair this with in a finally: an exception that skips the close would drop the accumulated writes, where the unbatched store had already persisted each one.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Data.SubdlSqliteContext.EndBatch
member.summary: Closes a batch and commits what it accumulated. Nested batches commit at the outermost close, so a caller opening one inside another cannot flush a half-finished unit of work.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Data.SubdlSqliteContext.RequestSave

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Data.SubdlSqliteContext.ConfigurePragmas
member.summary:
Sets the pragmas this store runs with. Called once per context, right after the schema exists.
journal_mode=WAL is set EXPLICITLY, because it is not the default: SQLite and Entity Framework both start in the rollback-journal mode (delete) — verified by reading PRAGMA journal_mode back on a fresh EF-created file, which answered delete. WAL is what this store wants: the plugin has one writer (a scheduled task, serialised by the global run lock) and several readers (the configuration page polls every 10 seconds, the diagnostics endpoint walks four areas), and in WAL a reader never blocks the writer or sees a half-written state.
The mode is stored IN the file, so this is a one-time change per database. It is also the reason the reset and restore paths must checkpoint before they copy the file: in WAL the committed writes sit in the side journal until a checkpoint, and a copy that ignores it is a backup missing everything since the last one.
busy_timeout covers the one case the in-process gate cannot: two CONTEXTS, or a second process, over the same file. SQLite then answers "database is locked" immediately; the timeout makes it wait instead of failing a scheduled run.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Data.SubdlSet`1
member.summary:
One area of the store, reached by the same verbs the previous engine offered — FindById, FindAll, Find, Upsert, DeleteMany, Exists, Count.
Why the predicates are evaluated in memory rather than handed to Entity Framework as SQL: the registries depend on that behaviour and say so. QaFailTracker compares languages with String.Equals(..., StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase), which no provider can translate, and the stored values are the plugin's own strings — a provider that translates the same comparison into SQL LIKE changes which rows match. A silent difference in matching is exactly the class of bug the registry code was written to avoid, so the comparison stays where it was: in LINQ-to-objects.
That is affordable because these areas are small — measured on a live install: 117 rows across all ten areas, the largest being 86 embedded tracks. Rows are read once per area, kept for the lifetime of the context, and invalidated on write, so a read costs a memory walk and a write one round trip.

member.name: F:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Language.LanguageMapper.ToIso6392Map
member.summary: F-M261: reverse of , from the SubDL two-letter code to the ISO 639-2/B code a Matroska track tag is written in.
member.remarks:
Only the languages the offline detector can actually return are listed: the tag writer needs this for exactly those, and a half-filled table invites the mistake of trusting it for the rest. Anything unmapped falls back to the lower-case two-letter code, which is a legal Matroska tag (ffprobe reports it unchanged, as it does for und) — a usable tag rather than a missing one.
The B spelling (not the terminological T form) is used on purpose: ger, fre, chi, cze, dut, gre, rum and slo are what these containers carry in practice and what ffprobe prints back; deu/fra would still be read correctly by but would read as a change against the file's own neighbours.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.LibraryScope
member.summary: Resolves the configured library selection to the concrete media PATHS it covers, so a selection keeps working when libraries are NESTED.
member.remarks: F-M189 (24.09.2026, user decision "das muss auch mit Unterverzeichnissen funktionieren"): a library whose path sits INSIDE another library's path (e.g. Test_SubDL = /data/movies2/Test_SubDL while Movies = /data/movies2) does not own its items in Jellyfin — the scan logs "Found duplicate path", the items stay in the OUTER library and GetCollectionFolders returns that outer name. A name-only comparison therefore never matches the inner selection: measured on the test server, selecting "Test_SubDL" queued 0 of 26 files while the items resolved to "Movies". Matching the item PATH against the selected libraries' locations fixes that without touching the library layout, and stays correct in the ordinary non-nested case (an item inside library X is under one of X's locations).

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.AiTranslatedSubs
member.summary:
F-M449: one SubDL account publishes machine-translated subtitles. Whether those uploads may be downloaded is a switch on its own (`Allow AI translated subs`, off by default), and the answer is applied to the SEARCH RESULT — a candidate from that account never enters ranking, never costs a download unit and never becomes a fallback for an item that has no other candidate.
The match runs on the uploader name of the API response, not on the release name and not on the entry title: the account is the one stable carrier, while a machine-translated release can be named anything. Spacing, dots, hyphens and underscores are removed before the comparison, so "SUBDL AI", "subdl_ai" and "SubDL.AI" all land on the same key; the comparison is EQUALITY, so a different account whose name merely starts the same way keeps its candidates.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.BrokenSubtitleReports
member.summary:
F-M450: what one report to SubDL says, and which of its four categories it lands in.
The text is DELIBERATELY bare. SubDL's report form offers four categories for a subtitle — "not a subtitle" (spam, fake, incomplete), "wrong release info", "stolen", "other" — and the operator asked for the naked finding, not for a justification: the package, what is wrong with it, and who reports. No request, no apology, no measurement history. Everything that is not the finding belongs in the attribution line, which is the same for every report.
The category follows the finding, never the caller: an empty package is an incomplete subtitle, a wrong runtime is "other" (nothing in the catalogue covers a mismatch of cut), and a wrong language is wrong metadata. A finding nobody can classify returns null and is not reported.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.DownloadBudget
member.summary:
F-M95 / F-M50: the ONE place that turns the candidate setting into the number the search and the download loop use.
There was a SECOND parameter here, keepBest (F-M242), which raised both numbers to the "best subtitles to keep per language" count. Both the setting and that raise are GONE (operator order 08.10.2026): a language now receives exactly one corrected file, and the walk's stop is no longer a user-tunable count. Keeping the parameter after removing the setting would have left a number in the signature that nothing can set — the same kind of dead knob F-M242 was created to fix.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.DownloadBudget.SearchEarlyStopThreshold(System.Int32)
member.summary:
F-M95 / F-M50 (operator order 08.10.2026): the ONE number the search width and the Auto-Sync walk both use, derived from the single setting "Auto-Sync attempts and max. download/search limit".
Two settings became one. The search's per-language width and the walk's stop were two knobs describing the same intent, and at their equal defaults the walk's cap was checked FIRST and counted the same attempts — so the cap always fired first and the correction budget could never trigger. Measured by replaying the loop: at 3/3 the cap stopped the walk in every ordering, and the budget only ever won when the cap was raised above it, which was the keep-best raise that went with F-M319.
The operator's rule is one setting with two effects: it decides how many candidates per language are searched and how many candidates the Auto-Sync may pull before it gives up.
There was a SECOND parameter here, keepBest (F-M242), which raised both numbers to the "best subtitles to keep per language" count. Both the setting and that raise are GONE (F-M319): a language now receives exactly one corrected file.
member.returns: The search's per-language width; 0 = no early stop.

F-M322 (operator order 08.10.2026): the operator's wording is that the statistics measure SUCCESSFUL auto-syncs only, so this counter covers the files that were really MOVED. A file the fit found nothing wrong with is NOT added here — it was not aligned, and counting it would make the row claim an alignment that never happened. Such files have their own counter ().

member.summary: F-M44 weighted release score: group match × WeightGroup + token overlap × WeightToken + min(dl,500) × WeightDownload.

BACKUP = v2 filename batch (POST /api/v2/files/search), only when the id search yields nothing (or the item carries no id). v2 id search is retired as a search path (its season/episode params are ignored server-side); the similarity ranking is token-based and episode-blind. member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.DownloadPipeline.CandidateAttempt
member.summary: Candidate download dispatcher. v2 candidates carry an nId → GET /api/v2/subtitles/{nId}/download?format=file (Bearer). v1-style zip urls (backup unpack_files already carry ready single-file urls on dl.subdl.com) → legacy DownloadSubtitleFileAsync with the url prefix logic.

F-M215: downloads the single file of a candidate that belongs to / .
F-M260: also reports WHERE the bytes came from, because a season or range pack carries one file per episode and EACH of those files states its own hearing-impaired flag — independently of the pack's own header, which is often the opposite of its contents (measured on Mo.S01.WEBRip.x265-ION265: header hi=false, all 8 files hi=true). That per-file flag was parsed and then never read, so a hearing-impaired file was saved as a plain .srt and recorded as hi=false. Since SidecarNaming.IsHearingImpairedToken accepts only sdh, such a file never counted as hearing impaired again — the F-M254 HI reader kept answering "absent" for a variant that was sitting on disk.
member.returns: The bytes, and the source they came from (null source = the candidate as a whole).
member.summary:
F-M388 (operator order 02.11.2026): every candidate leaves here with its invisible cues already gone. A cue that is on screen for a millimetre of time is dropped and the file is renumbered — the same rule the upload side has had since F-M382 — instead of the file being convicted by a gate for carrying one.
It happens HERE, before the gates and long before the write, because the state hash must describe the file that gets written. writeBytes starts as these very bytes and ComputeHash describes the normalized text; if the correction came later, the hash would describe a file that exists nowhere on disk.
member.param: Candidate being fetched (only for the log line).

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.DownloadPipeline.CorrectInvisibleCues(System.Byte[])
member.summary: F-M388: drops the cues nobody can read and renumbers what is left. Wraps , which is also what EncodeCanonical and ComputeHash use — one rule, so written bytes, hashed bytes and gated bytes are the same bytes. What comes out is always the CANONICAL form — UTF-8 without BOM, LF, no trailing blank line — for clean input as well, because the hash describes exactly that form. A clean file therefore keeps its cues and its text unchanged; only the byte style follows the canonical rule (a trailing newline is dropped by the same trim the upload side has always applied).
member.returns: Corrected payload, or null when nothing was fetched.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.DownloadPipeline.DecodeSrt(System.Byte[])
member.summary: Decode SRT bytes with BOM detection (UTF-8/UTF-16LE/UTF-16BE) before any QA parse. The old hard-coded UTF-8 read mangled valid UTF-16 files (live case Coherence.zh: valid file appeared cue-less → false-positive structure reject). No BOM → strict UTF-8 (same as before).
member.remarks: F-M187: this is the ONLY path from downloaded bytes to text. Every consumer (QA parse, runtime check, content hash) must go through it — a caller using Encoding.UTF8.GetString directly turns a UTF-16 payload into mojibake, and then the hash computed at download time no longer equals the hash the upload side computes later over the same file, so IsContentKnown misses and the file is uploaded again. The runtime check degrades silently as well: NUL bytes break the timecode regex, so it reports "matches" without actually checking.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.FfmpegTools
member.summary:
The one place that talks to ffmpeg (F-M261).
The binary lookup, the one-pass extraction and the language-tag write lived apart before this class existed: extraction sat in UploadPipeline only, so the download side had no way to read a container — which is exactly why untagged tracks could never be resolved there (F-M261). Two copies of the lookup would drift the way the four name parsers and the three HI readers did, so there is one copy here.
Deliberately ffmpeg and NOT mkvpropedit: the latter is faster (measured 0.05 s against 2.4 s on a 550 MB episode) but it is a native, architecture-bound binary (arm64 here, X64 on the prod Docker container) and it is not present on either machine. ffmpeg is already required for extraction, ships for every platform and costs one remux only for the files that actually carry an untagged track.

member.returns: Path to ffmpeg, or "ffmpeg" to let the OS report the failure.

member.summary: Locate an executable in PATH. Uses "where" on Windows, "which" elsewhere.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.FfmpegTools.ExtractAllAsync(System.String,System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Int32},Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILogger,Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Configuration.PluginConfiguration,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: F-M5: extract EVERY given subtitle stream of one file in a SINGLE ffmpeg call.
member.remarks:
Why one call and not one per stream: ffmpeg must open and (over CIFS/NAS) re-read the container for every invocation. On a 1 GB episode with 83 subtitle streams that is 83 reads of the same gigabyte — measured on prod 28.09.2026 as the only multi-minute stalls in an otherwise 11 s-median run. One call with repeated -map 0:s:N + -f srt output pairs reads the file once and writes one file per stream, so the container is read a single time however many streams it carries.
The mapping uses the SUBTITLE-relative index (0:s:N), never the container index: mixing the two lands on video/audio streams (exit 8 / no-stream errors). Callers pass positions computed against the unfiltered subtitle list.
member.returns: The extracted texts plus ffmpeg's exit code. A stream that produced no text maps to null. The exit code travels with the result because it is the difference between "this stream has no text" (0) and "the pass went wrong, retry it per stream" (non-zero) — the caller needs that to decide whether a null is a verdict or a suspicion.

member.summary: F-M261: writes a corrected language tag into the container for each given stream.

remarks.para: The remux copies every stream (-c copy), so no audio or video is re-encoded and the call costs one read of the file. Measured on the 550 MB Slow.Horses.S06E03: 2.4 s, byte-identical stream data.

WHY THIS MUST RUN BEFORE THE MEDIA HASH: the plugin's OSHash is size plus the first and last 64 KB of the file, and a Matroska segment header carries its own size — so writing a tag changes the hash. Measured on that episode: 550277727 bytes / 32d41dc3a0359d27 before, 550277733 bytes / 09eb61d402fba20b after. Changing the file after the hash was taken leaves every registry row hanging under an identity the file no longer has.

The write is atomic from the caller's point of view: ffmpeg writes a sibling temp file, the result is verified to carry the wanted tag, and only then is the original replaced. A failure at any step leaves the original untouched and returns false.

member.param: Container to edit, replaced in place.

F-M284: subtitle positions whose FORCED disposition must survive the rewrite. Written with the ADDITIVE form +forced, never the bare one — measured on a real container: -disposition:s:s:N forced CLEARS every other disposition of that stream (a stream carrying default=1 came back as default=0), while +forced leaves them untouched. The disposition is the only place a forced track is recorded, so a rewrite that dropped it would silently turn a forced track into the film's dialogue.
member.returns: True when the tags were written and verified.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.FfmpegTools.ReadSubtitleTagsAsync(System.String,System.String,Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILogger,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Reads the container's per-subtitle language tags through ffprobe.
member.remarks: The returned keys are SUBTITLE-RELATIVE positions, not container indices, because that is what -metadata:s:s:N writes and what callers hold. ffprobe reports the global index, so the subtitle streams are sorted by it and renumbered — comparing the two numberings directly would verify every position against the wrong stream and reject a write that actually succeeded.
member.param: Resolved ffmpeg binary; ffprobe is looked up next to it.
member.returns: Subtitle position to tag, or null when the list could not be read.

member.summary: True when a container tag matches the wanted ISO 639-2 code.
member.remarks: Matroska tags are free text, so a file may carry eng, en or English. The comparison accepts the two- and three-letter spelling of the same language rather than demanding byte equality, so a tag ffmpeg normalised is not mistaken for a failed write — which would throw away a good remux and redo it on every run.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.IPackFiller
member.summary:
F-M389 (operator order 02.11.2026): supplies the missing episode of a season that is otherwise ready for a pack.
A complete season used to dissolve into single uploads as soon as one of its episodes was not part of the current run — the episode was up already, so there was nothing to send for it, and the pack lost its eighth member. The filler closes that gap: for an episode nobody has queued, it returns the candidate a pack may carry, built from the subtitle that is already on SubDL.
The contract is deliberately narrow and fail-closed. A filler returns a candidate ONLY when the text it extracted passes the same gates the single upload path applies AND its content is already known to the registry — that is the proof that it was uploaded before. Anything else is null: an invented episode, a QA-failed subtitle or a never-uploaded track must never enter a pack, because the pack claims to be the complete season.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.LanguageTagGate
member.summary:
F-M261: the download quality gate that resolves untagged and 'und' subtitle tracks and — when enabled — writes the found language back into the container.
Both halves answer the SAME gap, which is why they are one gate rather than two features. A track whose tag is missing or und cannot be mapped: has no entry for und, so the two-letter fallback turns it into the invented language UN, and a null tag maps to nothing at all and gets no registry row. Either way the area reads "language absent" for a track that is sitting right there, and the item is queued and searched for a language it already carries.
Measured on Slow.Horses.S06E03 (30.09.2026): 44 text tracks, every one with lang=None. Extraction showed real content — English 48 KB, an SDH variant, Arabic, Portuguese, Bulgarian — so the file was fully subtitled while the registry read zero languages as present.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.LanguageTagGate.#ctor(Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILogger,Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Configuration.PluginConfiguration,Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry)

member.name: P:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.LanguageTagGate.DryRunActive
member.summary: True when a dry run is armed for EITHER direction, and the write half must therefore stand down (F-M22).
member.remarks: F-M263 (user decision 30.09.2026): both dry-run switches suppress the container rewrite, not just the one for their own direction. The reason is that this pass is not part of either pipeline's search work — it edits media FILES, and it runs from the seeder, which belongs to no direction at all: the seeder scans before both pipelines and is reached by every trigger. Tying the write to one switch would leave the other dry run rewriting the user's library, which is exactly what F-M22 forbids. Detection still runs in a dry run — the run's value is reporting what it WOULD do — so this gates the WRITE only, never the resolution.

member.remarks: The definition of "untagged" lives here and nowhere else. It matches what the upload pipeline has treated as undecided since F-M74: a NULL/empty tag means und, and so does the literal und/undefined. Keeping one copy is deliberate — the four name parsers and the three HI readers that existed in parallel all drifted.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.LanguageTagGate.RunAsync(System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{MediaBrowser.Model.Entities.MediaStream},System.String,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Resolves the language of every text track of one container, optionally writing the found languages back into the file.
member.param: Container to read, and to edit when the write half is on.
All subtitle streams of the item, UNFILTERED (as Jellyfin returns them).
member.returns: The resolution outcome. Never throws for a per-file failure.
member.remarks:
F-M264 (user order 30.09.2026, "bitte nur einmal"): a file whose tags this install already wrote is not written a second time. Measured on prod 30.09.2026 — Paris.Has.Fallen.S02E04 was rewritten twice inside one cycle, 8 s apart: the DOWNLOAD-seed pass wrote the codes, and the UPLOAD-seed pass that follows in the same cycle found the SAME tracks untagged and wrote them again. The second pass was not reading a stale value of its own: it asked Jellyfin, and Jellyfin caches its stream list — the container was corrected at 13:30:59, Jellyfin noticed the change only at 13:32:07 ("File changed, pruning extracted data"), after the cycle had ended. Every rewrite is a full remux of the media file (ffmpeg cannot edit a container in place), so the duplicate cost a second 540 MB copy, a second identity change and a second round of registry bookkeeping for five tags that were already in the file.
The skip is per TRACK and keyed on the tag the container was just verified to carry, which is the one fact the cached stream list cannot contradict. An untagged track stays work in any later run, so this cannot mask a genuine failure to write: the temp file is verified and only then moved over the original, so a track seen as tagged here is tagged on disk.

members.member:
The plugin's own log mode decides how much detail its lines carry, and every line says which of the three levels produced it.
Why not real levels: Jellyfin's Serilog pipeline filters a record BEFORE the sink sees it, so a line written at Debug never appears while the server sits at its default Information — and Trace ranks below Information, which is why the TMDb traces gated at Verbose reached no log at all (measured 0 [TRC] lines in a full production day). Everything here therefore goes out at INFORMATION, which the server always passes, and the level travels as a text marker instead: [N], [V] or [D] in front of the message.
Normal: lifecycle and summaries. Verbose: per-item work and the TMDb trace. Debug: internals, diagnostics and API traces. Warnings and errors are never gated and need no marker — Jellyfin's own level column already labels them.
F-M224: the plugin's own log mode is the only authority, and every line is written at a level Jellyfin always passes.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.MediaNameParser
member.summary: Derives the media TYPE and the season/episode numbers from a FILE NAME.
member.remarks: F-M190 (24.09.2026, user decision): the file name states what a file IS — "Serie.S01E05.1080p" is season 1, episode 5 — and that is more reliable than Jellyfin's folder classification. When an episode lives in a library typed "movies" (a perfectly normal setup, and exactly how the nested test library is configured), Jellyfin imports it as a Movie, so class-based type detection searches TMDB for a FILM named after the episode ("Norway No How") and finds nothing. The movies2 watchdog resolved this the same way: a regex over the name decides series-vs-movie, independent of any library setting.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.MediaNameParser.NeedsUnicodeFold(System.String)

members.member:
(user decision 25.09.2026): ONE lock for every state-mutating component — seeder, download, upload, postprocessing, database refresh, oshash-refresh. All six touch the same data store, so a single mutual exclusion is what the design needs.
Overlap is NOT waited out. A caller that cannot acquire gets false immediately and reschedules itself by JobSpacingMinutes (the scheduler coordinators already expose Schedule*Fire for this). The previous implementation polled a block file every 5 s for up to 10 minutes and logged a line per poll: measured on 21.09.2026 that produced 36 identical "already active" lines and a 3.5-minute stall while not preventing a single run (SkippedByLock never fired once).
Stale detection is retained and is the only reason the block file still exists: the file carries "PID|UTC timestamp" of the holder, so a run that died without cleanup (crash, hard kill) is detected two ways instead of waiting out a window — 1. the holder PID no longer exists → take over immediately; 2. the holder PID exists but the stamp is older than → a run wedged inside a living process; take over. A block file older than is taken over as a last resort.
Fail-open: a malformed or unreadable block file must never wedge the plugin.
F-M94h: ONE global run lock for all six state-mutating components. Overlap is never waited out: a caller that cannot acquire is refused at once and reschedules itself by the job spacing.

member.remarks: F-M380 (measured 01.11.2026, Dexter: Resurrection): the WIDTH decides, not the height. A cropped 1080p encode reads 1920x800, and 800 fell into the >= 700 bucket — the pack was named 720p while the file is 1080p class. member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.SeasonPack.ReleaseGroup(System.String)
member.summary: The release group a media file name states, if it states one. Nothing is invented: a name that ends in an episode title yields null, and so does a technical token such as -AAC5.1.
member.param: File name without extension, or a release name.
member.returns: Group token such as Rapta, or null.
member.remarks:
F-M430 (operator order 03.11.2026: "60 Prozent ist zuwenig"): the old rule — the last --segment and nothing else — read one of the four spellings the library uses. The reason for the misses was shape, not absence:
…x264-NeoNoir — dash.
…x264.YIFY — dot-separated (scene releases).
…HEVC x265 BONE, …(1080p AMZN WEB-DL x265 Ghost) — space-separated, sometimes inside brackets.
…x265-MeGusta[EZTVx.to], …x264.[MPup], …x264-[YTS.LT] — a site tag or a bracketed group behind the group.
The rule now: strip a trailing bracket or parenthesis (and read inside it only when the outside states nothing), then take the last token after -, . or a space — provided the token before it is a TECHNICAL token (codec, source, audio, resolution, bit depth, HDR, edition). That predecessor is what keeps an episode title out: …S01E03.OutKast has an episode tag in front of it, not a codec, so the answer stays null. A name that states no release at all states no group either — nothing is invented.

Pattern:
(?i)s\\d{1,2}[\\s._-]?e\\d{1,4}|\\d{1,2}x\\d{1,4}
Explanation:
○ Match with 2 alternative expressions, atomically.
○ Match a sequence of expressions.
○ Match a character in the set [Ss].
○ Match a Unicode digit greedily at least 1 and at most 2 times.
○ Match a character in the set [\-._\s] atomically, optionally.
○ Match a character in the set [Ee].
○ Match a Unicode digit atomically at least 1 and at most 4 times.
○ Match a sequence of expressions.
○ Match a Unicode digit atomically at least 1 and at most 2 times.
○ Match a character in the set [Xx].
○ Match a Unicode digit atomically at least 1 and at most 4 times.

member.summary:
The pack's identity: MD5 over the episodes' content hashes in episode order.
There is no container to hash — the ZIPPING IS SUBDL'S (the Upload API takes one file per call, collects their file_n_ids and uses the name field as the zip name on download). The identity therefore describes the same thing the zip would have: which subtitles, in which order, with which text. A corrected episode yields a new hash, so a corrected season is a new pack.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.SeasonPackCoordinator
member.summary:
F-M372: holds back the episodes of a complete season until the season is whole, then sends ONE pack instead of one upload per episode.
The two rules the operator set decide everything here: an incomplete season stays single, and so does a season whose episodes did not all pass the gates. The buffer therefore only ever collects; whether a pack happens is decided when it is full, and what is left over at the end of the run goes up the single way.
A pack is always one language, one HI flag, one source: lang, hi, quality, framerate and releases are single fields on SubDL's side, so mixed episodes cannot share a container.

F-M389 (operator order 02.11.2026): before that, an incomplete buffer is offered the filler. An episode whose subtitle is ALREADY on SubDL does not have to be in this run for the season to be a pack — it is fetched from the library, gated and proven, and then joins the buffer. member.summary:
F-M389: completes an incomplete buffer from the subtitles that are already uploaded, and sends it as a pack when every missing episode arrived.
The buffer always holds at least one NEW candidate — it exists only because something was added to it — so a season whose subtitles are all up never reaches this point, and no "nothing to send" branch is needed. What the filler adds is filler-only: it is asked per missing episode, in episode order, and the first null ends the attempt. Half a season is not a pack, and neither is a pack whose one doubtful member was quietly left out.

member.summary:
F-M389 (operator order 02.11.2026, revised the same day): packs a season the queue no longer touches at all — every episode is up already, so the run has nothing new to send and the pack consists of what the filler proves is already there.
The members are re-sent inside the container, which is how SubDL builds a pack; what the rule forbids is INVENTING one. Each member therefore comes from , which runs the single path's gates and demands the content be known. A season that cannot be completed from what is up sends nothing at all — there is no single upload to fall back to, because those subtitles are already on SubDL (that is why is asked not to dissolve a refused container into singles here).
member.param: SubDL language code the pack is built for.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.SourceQuality
member.summary:
F-M344 (operator order 10.10.2026): the SOURCE QUALITY an upload reports.
Until 10.10.2026 the metadata step sent the literal "web", with no reason recorded and no requirement asking for it — a leftover of the first upload implementation (F-M8). It was wrong for every file that is not a streaming source: the Dinosaurs episodes in the operator's library are 480p DVD x265 Panda rips and went to SubDL as WEB, and so does every BluRay or HDTV file. The field is what SubDL shows as the release's quality tag and what its own filters read, so a wrong value mislabels the upload for everyone who filters by quality.
THE VALUE LIST IS THE DOCUMENTED ONE, NOT AN INVENTED ONE. subdl.com/api-doc documents exactly five values for the upload field quality: web (Web release, streaming, WEB-DL), bluray, dvd, hdtv, cam. Measured on the live site: our own uploads (sent as web) are displayed with the tag webdl — the label differs from the value, the value is accepted. Anything this class cannot place stays web, which is exactly the behaviour that shipped before, so an unrecognized name cannot regress.
THE NAME IS THE EVIDENCE, and the loose file wins over the media file: for a sidecar the subtitle's own file name describes where THAT subtitle came from, while the media file next to it may be a different release of the same film. For an embedded track there is no own name — the container it was extracted from is the source, so the media file name is read.
THE LAST SOURCE WORD IN THE NAME WINS, and the words are matched as WHOLE TOKENS. A release name puts its title first and its source after it — The.DVD.Club.2019.1080p.BluRay.x264 is a BluRay, and the disc word belongs to the title. A substring rule would also read the CAM in "Cambridge" as a camera recording, which is why the short markers are never matched as fragments. The compact forms (for spellings whose separators swallow the word, "Blu-Ray") are consulted only when no token matched, and only against distinctive strings.
The asymmetry behind both rules: a missed BluRay falls back to web, which is the old behaviour; a false BluRay would mislabel a streaming release for everyone who filters. So the fallback is cheap and the false positive is not.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.StatusCounterDelta
member.summary:
F-M247 (user decision 28.09.2026: "Dryrun geht nie in die Statistik"): the cumulative counters a finished run contributes — with a dry run contributing nothing.
A dry run does real work: it searches, ranks, runs the id test and the QA gates, and every one of those steps bumps a counter in its summary. But it saves and uploads NOTHING. Letting those numbers through means the statistics report subtitles nobody wrote, which is what happened live on 28.09.2026 — 771 of the 858 "downloaded" entries came from one afternoon of dry runs.
The rule lives HERE and only here, because is the single writer of the statistics row. Gating the counters at each increment site would mean six places that can each drift; gating them once, at the boundary, means a new counter added later is either routed through this type or is visibly outside it.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.SubdlFramerate
member.summary:
F-M350 (operator order 18.10.2026): the framerate code an upload reports.
Until now the metadata step sent the literal "0", which SubDL documents as "default / unknown". That was not a decision, it was a leftover: the value was never wired, although the frame rate is already read in this codebase for the download-side FPS gate (F-M43 stage 1) and the item's video stream carries it. SubDL shows the field as the release's frame rate and its own filters read it, so sending "unknown" for a file whose rate is known makes the upload less findable than it could be — the same shape as the hardcoded quality that F-M344 replaced.
THE VALUE LIST IS SUBDL'S, NOT AN INVENTED ONE. Measured on the live search API across 120 subtitle entries: code 0 always arrives with fps: null, code 2 always with fps: 23.976 — the numeric codes are a table, and the numbers below are the ones the download side of this plugin already maps (SubdlApiClient, "0 = unknown; 2 ⇒ 23.976, 3 ⇒ 25, 4 ⇒ 29.97, 5 ⇒ 24, 7 ⇒ 30"). No other code was observed in the sample and none is invented here: a rate that is not in the table (48, 50, 59.94, 60 …) stays 0, which is exactly what shipped before, so an unusual rate cannot regress into a wrong claim.
NEAREST WINS. Container rates arrive as exact values (23.976023…, 29.970029…) and as the plain integers people expect (24, 25, 30), and 23.976 sits only 0.024 away from 24 — a fixed epsilon would have to be smaller than that and would then reject the float noise of the real values. So the closest table entry is chosen and a candidate further away than is refused. The two neighbours are 0.03 apart at worst, so nothing is ambiguous within tolerance.

member.summary: SubDL's "default / unknown" code. Also the answer for every rate not in the table.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.SubdlFramerate.CodeFor(System.Nullable{System.Double},System.Nullable{System.Double})
member.summary: Maps the item's video stream to SubDL's code, using the AVERAGE rate first and the REAL one as the fallback (operator order 18.10.2026 "dann bauen").
member.remarks:
Neither field is trustworthy on its own — measured over the operator's 2302 video files, they fail on different subsets: 27 files carry a broken average (1000) with a correct real rate, 18 carry a good average with a real rate that is 0.05+ off (29.9166), and 11 have both mapping to a DIFFERENT code (23.9756 ⇒ 2 against 24 ⇒ 5). With the fallback, 2257 of 2302 files report a code (98.0 %); average alone gives 96.8 %, real alone 97.3 %.
The average goes first because it is the PLAYBACK rate — frames divided by duration, which is what SubDL's fps means — while the real rate is only the timing grid (a file with every second frame dropped reports avg 12.6 against real 25). The download gate (F-M43 stage 1) reads the same order, so a file gets the same rate in the gate and in the upload. On the 11 conflicts the choice is therefore consistency, not truth: both readings are defensible and the difference only shows on music videos.
A broken average is not a rate: 1000 comes from containers that report one frame in one millisecond (reproduced with ffmpeg), so it is refused by the table and the real rate takes over.
member.param: The stream's average frame rate (0 when unknown).
The stream's real base frame rate (0 when unknown).
member.returns: One of .

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.UploadPipeline.ExtractAllStreamsAsync(System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Int32},System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: F-M5: extract EVERY text subtitle stream of one file in a SINGLE ffmpeg call.
member.remarks:
Why one call and not one per stream: ffmpeg must open and (over CIFS/NAS) re-read the container for every invocation. On a 1 GB episode with 83 subtitle streams that is 83 reads of the same gigabyte — measured on prod 28.09.2026 as the only multi-minute stalls in an otherwise 11 s-median run. One call with repeated -map 0:s:N + -f srt output pairs reads the file once and writes one file per stream, so the container is read a single time however many streams it carries.
The mapping uses the SUBTITLE-relative index (0:s:N), never the container index: mixing the two lands on video/audio streams (exit 8 / no-stream errors). Callers pass positions computed against the unfiltered subtitle list.
member.returns: The extracted texts plus ffmpeg's exit code. A stream that produced no text maps to null. The exit code travels with the result because it is the difference between "this stream has no text" (0) and "the pass went wrong, retry it per stream" (non-zero) — the caller needs that to decide whether a null is a verdict or a suspicion.

Two questions, two sources: what we hold comes from the library (every Episode item of the season, deduplicated by episode number — a two-part file carries one number), what aired comes from . A season nobody can answer for is not packed.

member.summary:
F-M389 (operator order 02.11.2026): one missing episode of a pack, taken from the subtitle that is already uploaded for it.
The order is the guarantee. The episode is resolved from the library, the text is extracted from its own file, canonicalised, and then put through the SAME gates as a normal upload; only a text that survives them AND is known to the registry — the proof that it went up before — becomes a candidate. Everything else returns null, which makes the coordinator send nothing rather than a pack with a hole in it.
It is deliberately not : that method's duplicate verdict is exactly what this one has to confirm, so it calls the gate half () and asks the registry itself.

HI/SDH variant the pack is built for.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Pipeline.UploadPipeline.PackPairsOf(MediaBrowser.Controller.Entities.BaseItem,System.String)
member.summary:
F-M420 (operator order 02.11.2026): the seasons a pack may be closed for at the END of a run — every episode is up, so a container is what is left to do.
Asked AFTER the item loop on purpose: at that point this run's own single uploads are in the store, which is exactly what makes a season packable ("erst einzelupload, dann staffelpack"). Asked before the loop instead, a season whose episodes went up minutes earlier looked unpackable and waited a whole cycle for its container.
The language is not invented: it is the one every episode of the season carries an UPLOADED row for, read from the registry per file. A season that is already a pack is left alone — its rows then carry the pack id — because sending the same container again every run is not a pack, it is a loop.
member.param: Complete seasons with their aired episode set.
member.returns: One entry per (season, language, variant) a pack may be attempted for.

member.summary: F-M467 (measured 11.11.2026 on VisionQuest tt23112594): the IDS OF THE SERIES, and the series is resolved even when the episode does not carry it. Episode.Series is a convenience that is NULL for items read as children of a season folder — which is exactly how the pack phase reads a season it did not work this run. Every per-FILE language check then compared against a null id, answered "no" for every language, and no pack was built although the files carried 25 languages in all eight episodes. member.param: Path of the plugin configuration file.
Field name to value. Null values are skipped, not written as empty.

F-M438 (measured 04.11.2026): the declaration order of the configuration properties. Jellyfin's XML serializer matches elements in the order the class declares them, so an element that does not exist yet has to be INSERTED at its declared position. Appending it to the end of the document — which is what this writer did — puts it after later members and the value is silently ignored on the next load: exactly one restart, then the field reads as unset again.
member.returns: True when the file was written.

member.summary: Recreate the shared data context after a reset/restore.

members.member:
Gets the plugin description (shown in Dashboard → Plugins).
This string is compiled into the DLL and is what the plugin card renders — NOT build.yaml, which only feeds the catalog manifest. Keep it to two sentences: the card is a one-glance summary, not a feature list or an explanation of the id resolution design (that lives in F-M203/F-M219 and the README).
F-M220/F-M221: this string and build.yaml must hold the same text, under 320 characters, and must name both required keys. The card reads the DLL, not build.yaml. Operator order 10.10.2026: the card carries the AI disclosure as its last sentence. The card and the catalogue therefore say the same thing; the catalogue reads it from build.yaml, and a Jellyfin with the plugin installed copies this text into its own meta.json at install time — so a card without the sentence would hide it exactly where the plugin is in use.

member.name: F:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Plugin.SharedDbContextLock
member.summary: Guards the lazy creation of the shared context.
member.para: Without this, two scheduled tasks starting in the same tick both see _sharedDbContext == null and each construct a SubdlDbContext over the same data file. The engine then in use had a non-thread-safe object mapper, so the concurrent schema setup raced and one task died with System.NotSupportedException: Member Id not found on BsonMapper for type EmbedTrackEntity (measured 26.09.2026 at 08:21:09.081/.082, prune and OSHash firing in the same scheduler tick — the first occurrence in any log). The task itself is fine: started alone it completes normally.

The lock is kept although the engine changed: two contexts over one SQLite file is still a race this design does not want — the second one sees a half-initialised schema, and the shared instance is what every registry was handed at construction.

Jellyfin's own version, read from the loaded server assembly. Null when unavailable (unit test host, stripped build) — the caller stores null rather than inventing a value.
(25.09.2026, measured): the server assembly is named jellyfin (lower case, from jellyfin.dll) — Jellyfin.Server is only a NAMESPACE inside it, and there is no assembly by that name. The earlier probe therefore never matched and the recorded field was always null while the server was running normally. member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.AutoSyncWorker.IsMeasurementFailure(System.String)
member.summary:
F-M323: whether the worker was UNABLE TO MEASURE, as opposed to measuring and declining.
One predicate, matched on the exact prefixes returns, because that is the only place the distinction exists. A missing ffmpeg and undecodable audio are machine facts; fit error is the fit throwing. All three are RED on the worker's row — something is broken — while a measurement that declined is grey: nothing is broken, the file simply needed no correction.
The three audio/tool prefixes are the same set excludes, deliberately: there is one definition of "this says nothing about the file". not measured: only N cues is NOT here — it is a verdict on the file (F-M318).
member.returns: True when the worker could not measure at all.

member.name: F:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.DriftGate.SampleRate
member.summary:
Sample rate for the mono envelope decode.
F-M307: 16 kHz, not 8 kHz. At 8 kHz the Nyquist limit is 4 kHz, so the 300–3400 Hz voice band-pass keeps almost the whole spectrum and filters nothing — measured, the probability curve then came out FLATTER (correlation 0.996 against the validated reference, mean |difference| 0.010) and the flattening is what decides whether a short step is kept or dropped. At 16 kHz the band-pass has room to work.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.DriftGate.ParseCuesWeighted(System.String)
member.summary: Cue times PLUS a per-cue weight, in the same order as . Weight 0 marks a line the offset fit must not score on: music (♪) and sound labels ([door slams], GUNSHOT). Such a cue still gets MOVED by its segment's shift — it belongs to the same time frame as the dialogue around it — but it may not vote on where the steps go, and it may not inflate the segment charge Z·σ·√(cues). Measured on Line.of.Fire S01E02: with music labelled in the score the fit collapsed a real 6 s drop into ONE step and sat 3 s off for four minutes; the same cues at weight 0 let it split the drop into the two 3 s steps that the plain subtitle shows.
member.returns: Starts, ends and weights (1.0 = scored, 0.0 = music/sound label).

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.DriftGate.IsSpeechCue(System.String)
member.summary: F-M360: gefittet wird nur auf Dialogzeilen; Musik, Klammer-Lautlabels und nackte Großbuchstaben-Lautwörter werden nicht bewertet, aber mitverschoben. Whether a subtitle line carries spoken dialogue, i.e. whether the offset fit may score on it. Music lines (♪/♫), bracketed sound labels ([door slams], {phone rings}) and bare capitalised sound words (GUNSHOT) are not speech: they sit on music or effects, vote the same at nearly every candidate offset, and so dilute the evidence and inflate the segment charge.
member.returns: true when the line is dialogue.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.DriftGate.DecodeFrameLevelsAsync(System.String,System.String,System.Threading.CancellationToken,System.String)
member.summary:
Frame levels (dB) from a band-passed mono decode, WITHOUT ever holding the samples. The raw f32le stream is read in chunks and the energy of each frame is accumulated on the fly.
This is what the two consumers actually need: and both walk the samples frame by frame and compute nothing but 20*log10(sqrt(mean(v^2))). Nothing reads an individual sample outside that loop, so materialising the samples buys nothing and costs a lot: for a 140-minute track the old path held a 514 MB byte[] AND a 514 MB float[] at the same time — measured ~1 GB peak, which the OOM killer took (exit 137 on the 140-minute files). Streaming the same track holds 3.2 MB.
member.returns: One dB level per frame; an empty array when the audio is unusable.

member.name: F:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.OffsetFit.DeployZ
member.summary:
Significance the deploy rule demands of the cues the fit MOVES, in standard errors of their mean gain. Separate from on purpose: that one is the DP charge and shapes the segments, this one only decides whether the result is written.
Measured on 34 real fits of one series (one morning, all language variants), against the operator's own listening verdicts: every file he reported as audibly WRONG sat at t = 1.06 / 1.15 / 1.38 / 1.51, every file he confirmed as GOOD at t = 2.66 and 8.45. Nothing sits between 1.51 and 2.66, so the gap separates the two groups completely, while = 1.0 let all four bad files through — they cleared it by a hair and were written. At 2.0 the four are refused (left as downloaded) and no good file is lost.
This is a threshold fitted on the run it judges, which this class's own notes warn against — but the failure it catches is not a subtle one: those fits had landed on the wrong piece of sound (adjacent-segment jumps of 10.25-34.00 s against at most 5.50 s for the good ones), so a weak paired test is the observable symptom of a wrong fit. Watch for a run of refusals; re-derive the bound as verdicts accumulate.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.OffsetFit.GuardOrder(System.Double[],System.Double[],System.Double[])
member.summary:
Applies the order guard to the per-cue shifts: no cue overtakes its predecessor's end. A cue that would land below zero is clamped by the writer, not here.
This runs BEFORE the deploy rule decides, and that order is load-bearing. At a step the two neighbours move by different amounts, and a step wider than the gap between them would push the earlier cue's end past the later cue's start — which a player renders as stacked text. The guard therefore pulls individual cues away from their segment's value, and those pulled values are what the deploy rule must score. Measured on the confirmed-good BCS file: without the guard the rule saw 118 moved cues and t = +2.74 and APPLIED the correction, while the reference — which guards first — saw 114 cues and t = +0.325 and correctly REFUSED it.
The bound is a LOWER one, because the shift is ADDED: eff[k] ≥ eff[k−1] − gap + MinGapSec. A gap already below the floor must not be shrunk further — measured, 560 of 724 gaps in this material are under 0.04 s with a median of 0.002 s, so demanding the floor everywhere carries one shift through the whole file.
member.returns: The number of cues the guard touched.

member.summary: Exposes the measured sigma (the median absolute score change per grid step), so a cross-language test can compare the two implementations' inputs, not just their output. A disagreement there points at the table; agreeing inputs with different output points at the fit.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.OffsetFit.ClassifyCause(System.Int32,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary:
F-M307 (order 18.10.2026): names WHY a fitted correction was refused. Pure, so the decision table is testable without decoding audio — the dry run over the real library caught this table putting a clearly-worse correction (t = -3.74, score 0.5032 -> 0.4914) into the hunting class.
Significance settles the class (operator 18.10.2026: "Signifikanz über 2 ist Pflicht für verbesserte subs"). There is no such thing as a MATERIAL score improvement without significance: +0.0131 at t = +1.54, +0.0076 at t = +1.71 and +0.0036 at t = +0.57 are all under 2 and therefore prove nothing — they are "not sufficiently evidenced", which keeps the reserved 9x and pulls the next candidate. Only a SIGNIFICANT worsening (t <= -DeployZ: untreated better) or a difference too small to matter (shift below the floor) is "no proven gain", where the file stays untouched.
The score can still veto, but ONLY where it decides: a correction with t > 2 that would lower the score is refused as "worse". Everywhere else the score is reported, not consulted — a lower score at t = -1.59 is not evidence of anything, so it stays "not sufficiently evidenced" (hunt), which is exactly the distinction the operator drew. The refused set stays the same as before the split — {t <= DeployZ} ⊇ {t <= -DeployZ} — so only the label moved, never which corrections get deployed.
member.param: Number of cues the fit would move.
Score of the file as it is.
t statistic over the moved cues.
member.returns: The cause; means the correction is applied.

member.name: F:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.QaGates.LangFamilyMap
member.summary: (user decision 10.09.2026): family exceptions for the F-M15 language gate. Some stream-tag languages are either (a) so close to a relative that the CLD2 detector legitimately lands on the relative, or (b) not supported by CLD2 at all, so the content is FORCED to be attributed to some neighbouring language — in both cases a "mismatch" verdict would reject perfectly fine subtitles. A reject now requires the detected language to lie OUTSIDE the family. Live cases that motivated this (registry 10.09.2026): MS->ID (Bahasa pair, 17×), CA->ES / GL->ES (Iberian neighbours), EU->ID (CLD2 has no Basque). Deliberately NOT included: main languages (DE/EN/NL/FR/IT/ES/PT/RU/PL...) — real mismatches there stay rejects.

member.summary: F-M307: corrects a downloaded subtitle by the piecewise-constant offset fitted against the audio. The fit is the only correction route (OffsetFit).

member.summary: Largest shift the feature will apply, in seconds. Beyond this the finding is treated as implausible.

member.name: F:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.SubtitleSync.MinShiftSec
member.summary:
Below this the file is not moved, in seconds.
Measured, not chosen: a subtitle file that nothing is wrong with still measures a small nonzero offset against its own audio, because a cue leads the speech onset by a per-cue varying amount. That is this material's measurement floor, and it is the same order as a small real offset, so a lower floor MOVED files that were already in sync. At 1.0 s a finding is at least twice the floor, and the fit additionally has to prove a gain (see OffsetFit's deploy rule), so the floor is a backstop rather than the decision.
member.remarks: 1.0 s until 18.10.2026, when the operator weighed the two ends ("1 Sekunde ist zuviel, 0.2 Sekunden zuwenig") and set 0.7. The measured floor of the reference episode's own in-sync subtitle is about 0.5 s, so 0.7 keeps a 0.2 s margin over what is normal and no longer refuses a real half-cue finding. Do not go below the floor: at 0.20 s the feature MOVED a file that was already correct (caught by the end-to-end test, not by reasoning).

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.SubtitleSync.RefusalIsCandidateSpecific(System.String)
member.summary:
F-M318 (operator order 08.10.2026): whether a refusal says something about THE CANDIDATE or about the AUDIO/tooling.
This is what separates a hunt worth continuing from quota spent for nothing. The fit refuses for two kinds of reason, and they look identical in the log:
a verdict on the FILE ("no proven gain", a shift beyond the limit, too few cues) — another candidate may well align, so the download repeats;
a verdict on the AUDIO or the tooling ("ffmpeg not available", "audio decode failed", "no audio samples") — every candidate would be refused for exactly the same reason, so walking on burns the daily quota to reach an identical answer.
The tool/audio reasons are therefore matched by their exact prefix and answered false. Everything else is treated as candidate-specific: a verdict this method does not know is more likely about the file than about the machine, and refusing to retry a fixable file is the worse error of the two.
member.returns: True when fetching another candidate could produce a different answer.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.SubtitleSync.RefusalMeansAlreadyGood(System.String)
member.summary:
F-M321 (operator order 08.10.2026): whether a refusal means the file needs NO correction.
"no proven gain" is the deploy rule DECLINING to move the file: nothing had to move, the correction would make the file worse, or the needed shift sits below the measurement floor. In every one of those cases the file AS DOWNLOADED is the best version of that language there is, and the operator's rule is that it is then treated like a correction — the walk ENDS (no quota spent hunting a candidate that cannot beat a file the fit found nothing wrong with) and the file takes the corrected range.
Every OTHER refusal keeps the F-M318 hunt alive: a file that is WRONG (a shift beyond the limit, too few cues, a first cue that would go negative) and — order 18.10.2026 — a correction that is gain not statistically proven, where the evidence is missing rather than the file being good or bad. Matched by exact prefix, like : this class composes the reason itself, so the prefix is the contract rather than a guess at wording.
member.returns: True when the refusal means the file is already the best available version.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.SubtitleSync.BuildRefusalReason(Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.OffsetFit.FitResult)
member.summary:
F-M307 (order 18.10.2026): names the condition that refused the correction and carries the numbers the decision was made on — the measured segments, the moved cues, the significance and the score the measurement reached.
TWO classes, and the difference decides whether another candidate is fetched (operator order 18.10.2026): "statistisch nicht ausreichend belegt" is NOT "no proven gain". A correction that improves the score but cannot prove it (NotSignificant) is a verdict about the EVIDENCE, not a statement that the subtitle is right — the original is kept in the reserved block and the next candidate is pulled. no proven gain stays for the three cases where the file really is the best there is: nothing had to move, the correction would make it worse, or the shift is too small to matter (below the floor).
member.param: The fitted result whose revert is being reported.
member.returns: The reason string; only the "no proven gain" shapes mean the file is already good.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.SubtitleSync.ShiftByStaircasePerCue(System.String,System.Double[])
member.summary:
Applies a PER-CUE shift list: cue k moves by [k].
F-M307 produces the shift per cue rather than per segment, because the order guard pulls individual cues away from their segment's value at a step. Applying the guarded values directly is what makes the written file identical to the one the deploy rule scored — recomputing a staircase from segment offsets here would silently re-introduce the very difference the guard exists to remove.
member.param: One shift per cue, in cue order.
member.returns: (ok, shifted text, reason).

member.name: F:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.SubtitleSync.MinGapSec
member.summary:
Minimum gap kept between one cue's end and the next cue's start, in seconds.
The same reasoning applies as on the anchor route this constant once came from: these subtitles butt cue against cue — measured, 560 of 724 gaps are below 0.04 s with a median of 0.002 s. A guard set tighter would fire on almost every cue.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Qa.SubtitleSync.ShiftByStaircase(System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Double},System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Double})
member.summary:
Applies a STAIRCASE shift: each cue is moved by the offset of its OWN segment (F-M300). This is what repairs a drifting file, where one constant offset cannot.
Segment k covers the cues from [k] up to the next entry, so a cue belongs to the last segment that starts at or before it.
The order guard is against the previous cue's END, exactly as the anchor path does it: at a step the two neighbours shift by different amounts, and a step wider than the gap between them would otherwise make the earlier cue's end land after the later cue's start — which a player renders as stacked text. Where the guard bites, the previous shift is carried forward, so the step is absorbed at that cue instead of inverting the order.
member.param: Segment start times, ascending; first is the file start.
One measured offset per segment, same length.
member.returns: (ok, shifted text, reason, steps actually kept) — the last is the count of order-guard bites.

member.name: T:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry
member.summary:
Persistent state of the subtitle pipeline, split by the kind of thing being described:
video files — area 2, keyed by media hash
embedded tracks — area 2 beneath the file, keyed by media hash + position
sidecar files — area 3, keyed by content hash
burned download candidates — area 4, keyed by item + language + SubDL id
Two rules hold everywhere in this class:
F-M194b: every area is keyed by a computed business key stored in the record's own id, never by a database-assigned auto id. 1. A row is written under a computed business key, never the database's auto id. The previous implementation upserted new SubtitleEntity { Id = 0 }; the store resolved an upsert by _id, so zero never matched and every write inserted. That produced 1277 rows for 782 facts (F-M194) and is structurally impossible now.
2. The stored state is the outcome, not the process. A subtitle is uploaded, rejected or downloaded — there is no separate "settled" row beside it saying the same thing twice, because every reader then has to know both layers and keep them consistent. "Is this position finished?" is derived by asking whether any of the three outcome states is present.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.DropInvisibleCues(System.String)
member.summary: Drops cues that are too short to be seen and renumbers the rest (operator decision 01.11.2026). One 1 ms cue (a doubled ♪ MTV ♪ line at 3.898 s) made the whole file fail qa-invalid-srt — measured on MobLand S01E02 — and thereby cost the ENTIRE season pack: 9 of 10 episodes were left, so every episode went up as a single and E02 not at all. Nobody watching is bothered by such a cue, the rule that judged it cost far more than the cue.
member.returns: The same text when nothing was dropped, otherwise the text without those cues.

members.member:
MD5 of the normalized content, in SubDL's own format: the hash of exactly the bytes that get uploaded. Deliberately MD5 — SubDL stores the md5 of the file as received, so any other algorithm would make the two sides incomparable by construction.
Raw SRT content. Lowercase 32-character hex hash. F-M17c2: remote duplicate detection needs BOTH the canonical payload (F-M185) and this function (F-M186); either one alone makes the comparison meaningless.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.EncodeCanonical(System.String)
member.summary: Encodes SRT content in the canonical form: UTF-8, no BOM, LF line endings, trailing whitespace trimmed — exactly the bytes the registry hash describes.
member.returns: The bytes to write to disk.
member.remarks: Operator order (07.10.2026): a file this plugin CHANGES is written normalized, so the form on disk is the form that was hashed. Writing the corrected file in the fetched payload's own byte style made the stored hash describe a byte sequence that existed nowhere on disk: same text, but BOM and CRLF put back on the way out. The two are equal only because NormalizeSrt happens to strip exactly what the style re-adds — an invariant nobody had asserted. Normalizing on the way out makes written bytes and hashed bytes identical BY CONSTRUCTION, with nothing to re-derive. The fetched original is NOT touched by this: it stays byte-for-byte as received inside the one-entry archive (F-M306), because that artefact exists precisely to be the uncorrected file.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.ReplaceMediaIdentity(System.String,System.String)
member.summary:
F-M261: moves a media file's whole registry state from its old hash to its new one.
The OSHash covers size plus the first and last 64 KB, and a Matroska segment header carries its own size — so writing a language tag into a container changes the file's identity. Every row of that file is keyed by the hash (media, embeds, sidecars), and without this move the file would keep TWO identities: the rows under the old hash stay, because nothing prunes them — only removes a media row whose JELLYFIN ITEM is gone and the item is still there, and the path-based prune is never called. Measured on a real rewrite: two media rows for one file, same item id, same path, with the download marks and every embed row left on the dead one.
The move is the union of both sides where they collide, and the OLD row wins: what stands under the old hash was earned by work on this same file, while a row under the new hash can only come from a run that already touched the rewritten file. Verdicts and observations are carried over unchanged — this is a rename, not a re-decision.
Same hash on both sides is a no-op, and an empty hash is refused: a hash that could not be computed must never act as if it were one.
member.param: Hash the file had before it was rewritten.
member.returns: Number of rows moved or merged.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.ObserveEmbed(System.String,System.Int32,System.String,System.Boolean,System.Boolean)
member.summary:
F-M257: records what a track IS (language, HI at this position) without touching a verdict.
The embedded area's only writer used to be , called exclusively by the upload pipeline — so on a default install (UploadEnabled=false) the area stayed empty and every registry reader of it answered from nothing. The seeder scans every item anyway and holds the streams in its hand; this method lets that fact be recorded where the readers look.
A verdict, once written, is never overwritten here: sets Status/Reason unconditionally, so calling it from an observer would erase an uploader's "uploaded"/"rejected" verdict with an observation. A fresh row is created as , which no terminality check counts.
member.param: F-M284: true when the track is forced (recorded, never coverage).
member.returns: True when a row was created or its facts changed.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.MarkDetectionAttempt(System.String,System.Int32,System.String,System.String,System.Boolean)
member.summary:
Records that language detection ran for this track and how it ended.
Deliberately NOT a MarkEmbed call: that one sets Status/Reason unconditionally, and a detection attempt is a fact about the WORK, not a verdict about the subtitle. Writing it through MarkEmbed would stamp rejected on the row, which the file-completeness arithmetic reads as terminal and would count as a settled track. Only the two detection fields are touched, everything else on the row is left as it is.
A row that does not exist yet is created as with an empty language, exactly like an observation: the language is unknown, which is the truth.
member.param: Detected language when one was found, else null.
HI/SDH verdict for the track, when the caller knows it.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.DetectedPositions(System.String)
member.summary:
The stream positions of this file whose language detection has already run.
The gate asks this BEFORE touching the container: extraction plus classification is the expensive half, and a track the detector could not classify would otherwise be re-opened on every single scan. Keyed on the presence of the attempt, not on its outcome — a track that resolved successfully needs no second look either.
The set is only as good as the identity it hangs from. A tag write rewrites the container, the hash changes, and the new hash has no rows yet, so the next scan legitimately retries.
member.returns: Attempted positions.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.RecordedPairs(System.String)
member.summary:
F-M282: every subtitle datum the registry records for this file — embedded rows and sidecar rows, each with its own language and its own hearing-impaired flag.
This used to be HearingImpairedLanguages: a set of LANGUAGE CODES, answering "which languages have a variant". That projection is exactly what the paired model removes — a language-keyed answer cannot distinguish the regular file from its variant, so a caller asking "is the German variant here?" was told about German and the regular subtitle was fetched over the file already on disk.
Both areas are consulted because a datum arrives either way: an embedded track the uploader or the observer stored (MarkEmbed, F-M257), or a sidecar the downloader fetched (MarkDownloaded).
F-M256: the parameter is the media PATH, not the hash. Every caller holds a path, and this method resolved nothing: handing it a path where a hash was expected made every lookup miss, so it returned an empty set for a file whose rows existed and every language read as "HI absent". Measured on prod 30.09.2026: 14 items whose container already carried an embedded SDH track were searched again. The hash is resolved HERE, once, so no caller can pass the wrong kind of value again — the mistake is not repairable by a caller, it is impossible.
member.returns: Pairs recorded for this file, from its embedded rows and its sidecar rows.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.RecordedPairsByHash(System.String)
member.summary:
F-M282: the pairs recorded under a known media hash.
Split out from the path-taking sibling so a caller that already holds the hash — or a host-free test whose media path does not exist on disk — can ask the same question without going through the oshash cache.
member.returns: Pairs recorded for this hash.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.EmbeddedLanguages(System.String)
member.summary: F-M263: the languages recorded for a file's EMBEDDED tracks — read from the registry, not from the stream list.
member.remarks:
The download pipeline's coverage check used to ask Jellyfin for the item's streams through `SidecarNaming.EmbeddedPresentLanguages`, and that answer is a CACHED snapshot: a container the seeder corrected in the same cycle still reports its OLD tag, so the language read as absent and the file was searched for a subtitle it demonstrably carries. The gate call in the pipeline existed only to paper over that with its own in-memory `_resolvedLanguages`, and it brought two defects with it (no hash pair, so no identity move; and a rewrite that no dry run stopped). With the gate gone from the pipeline, the record the SEEDER wrote is the authority — and unlike the stream list it is current, because the seeder wrote it from the gate's own verdict after the file was rewritten.
The hash is resolved from the path HERE, once — the same rule F-M256 established for : every caller holds a path, and a method that expects a hash while being handed a path misses every lookup without a compiler error.
Forced and bitmap tracks are excluded by the writers, not here: a forced track is not the film's subtitle (F-M246) and a bitmap track carries pixels (F-M257). Only rows that exist are read, and no row is written for a track the gate could not decide.
member.returns: Language codes recorded for embedded tracks.

member.summary:
F-M259: records what a loose subtitle FILE is, without touching a verdict.
The sidecar half of , and the same gap: is the area's only writer and only the upload and download pipelines call it, both behind their own switch (upload is off by default). A .srt beside the media that no plugin run ever moved — written by another tool, kept from before the registry existed, or simply never touched because upload is off — therefore had no row at all. The download side reads the disk for "is the language there?" but asks the REGISTRY for the HI question (F-M254), so such a file's language looked present and its hearing-impaired variant looked absent, run after run.
A verdict is never overwritten here, for the same reason as on the embedded side: sets Status unconditionally, so observing through it would erase an uploader's or downloader's verdict. A fresh row is created as .

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.MoveSidecarLocation(System.String,System.String,System.String)
member.summary:
Points an existing sidecar row at the file's new name after that file was renamed (F-M278).
A rename changes neither the content nor the verdict — the content hash is the row key and it does not move — so this updates the two location fields ONLY and returns early for a row that does not exist. It must never go through or the verdict writers: those rewrite Status, and an uploaded row silently downgraded to observed is the exact overwrite this class warns about.
It is not cosmetic. The refresh task forgets a sidecar row whose stored path no longer exists (), so a rename that left the old path behind would hand the reconciliation pass a "vanished file" and destroy the row for a file that is very much there — under a new name.

member.name: M:Jellyfin.Plugin.SubdlScribe.Registry.ContentHashRegistry.ForgetStaleEmbeds(System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{System.ValueTuple{System.Int32,System.String,System.Boolean,System.Boolean}},System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyCollection{System.Int32})
member.summary:
F-M258: embedded rows of a file that no longer match any track of that file.
A sidecar has a FILE beside the media, so its evidence can be probed with (). An embedded track has no file — its evidence is the stream list, which only a caller holding the item can read.
F-M266 (30.09.2026): this sweep is for OBSERVATIONS, and a VERDICT is out of its reach. The comparison below is only meaningful for a row whose language the caller's stream list can name. An untagged track is invisible to that list BY CONSTRUCTION — the shared reader (SidecarNaming.EmbeddedTracks) drops every position whose tag does not map — so a row for such a track looked "stale" on every single run and was deleted. That destroyed two kinds of work: the uploader's own verdict (rejected / und-too-small, stored with Language="UN") and the detection attempt record, both of which exist precisely for the tracks that cannot be resolved. Losing the first re-opens a settled question; losing the second re-opens the media file. Neither is this method's business.
Hence: a terminal row (uploaded/rejected) and a row carrying a detection attempt are kept unconditionally. Only plain observations are judged on their facts. The cost is that a verdict for a stream that has genuinely disappeared stays on disk; that is the cheap side of the trade, and the hash changes when a file is really rewritten, which retires the row through the identity move instead.
member.param: The tracks the file has NOW, as (position, language, HI).
member.returns: Removed rows.
